docs.title: Getting started with Pret
docs.text: Pret lets you build interactive interfaces in Python, inside notebooks or as standalone web applications. Use a Store to share data between components, connect edits to Python and save your work. The interface runs in the browser using React.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
pip install pret pret-joy

To use it with Jupyter, if you install the library in a custom environment (conda, venv, or other), you will likely need to tell Jupyter where to find the front-end files. You can do this by running the following command (only once):

pret update-jupyter-config --apply

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
• Python, only Python: pret is written in Python: you can write your both your UI and server actions Python. No need to learn a new language.
  • Client-side rendering: unlike other Python UI frameworks, pret runs primarily in the browser. This enables a fast response time to user actions (like hover events), and a better user experience under degraded network conditions.
  • Built on React: pret uses React as a rendering engine, and benefits from its ecosystem.
  • Reactive: unlike other solutions like ipywidgets, pret is reactive. Only the parts of the UI that need to be updated are re-rendered.
  • State management: in addition to React's local state management (i.e. use_state), pret provides a global and modular state management solution that is synchronized both between components, and between the client and the server.
  • Modular: pret is designed to be modular. You can easily create your own components, and reuse them in other pret-based projects.
  • Integrated with Jupyter: pret components can be used in Jupyter notebooks, as well as in standalone web applications.
  • Remote execution: pret can call and use the result of Python functions on the server from the browser

docs.title: Use it in a notebook
docs.text:
Let's write a simple todo app that should:

  • display a list of todos, that can be checked as done
  • display the number remaining todos
  • change the font to bold as a todo is hovered
  • allow editing the todo list directly in Python

Copy and paste the following code in a notebook:

from pret import component, create_store, run, use_state, use_store_snapshot
from pret_joy import Checkbox, Input, Stack, Typography

state = create_store(
  {
    "faire à manger": True,
    "faire la vaisselle": False,
  },
)


@component
def TodoApp():
  todos = use_store_snapshot(state)
  typed, set_typed = use_state("")
  num_remaining = sum(not ok for ok in todos.values())
  plural = "s" if num_remaining > 1 else ""

  def on_key_down(event):
    if event.key == "Enter":
      state[typed] = False
      set_typed("")

  return Stack(
    *(
      Checkbox(
        label=todo,
        checked=ok,
        on_change=lambda e, t=todo: state.update({t: e.target.checked}),
      )
      for todo, ok in todos.items()
    ),
    Input(
      value=typed,
      on_change=lambda event: set_typed(event.target.value),
      on_key_down=on_key_down,
      placeholder="Add a todo",
    ),
    Typography(
      f"Number of unfinished todo{plural}: {num_remaining}",
      sx={"minWidth": "230px"},  # just to avoid jittering when it's centered
    ),
    spacing=2,
    sx={"m": 1},
  )


TodoApp()

In comparison, the closest alternative using ipywidgets looks like the following snippet:

IPyWidget's implementation 
import ipywidgets as widgets

state = {
    "faire à manger": True,
    "faire la vaisselle": False,
}


class IPWTodoApp:
    def __init__(self):
        self.box = widgets.VBox()
        self.render()

    def _repr_mimebundle_(self, *args, **kwargs):
        return self.box._repr_mimebundle_(*args, **kwargs)

    def render(self, *args, **kwargs):
        num_remaining = sum([not checked for _, checked in state.items()])
        plural = "s" if num_remaining > 1 else ""

        def on_input_submit(sender):
            state[input_widget.value] = False
            self.render()

        def create_todo_item(todo, checked):
            def update_todo_status(*args, **kwargs):
                state[todo] = checkbox.value
                self.render()

            checkbox = widgets.Checkbox(
                value=checked,
                description=todo,
                disabled=False,
                indent=False,
            )
            checkbox.observe(update_todo_status, names="value")
            return checkbox

        input_widget = widgets.Text(
            placeholder="Add a todo",
            description="",
            disabled=False,
        )
        input_widget.on_submit(on_input_submit)

        self.box.children = [
            *(create_todo_item(todo, checked) for todo, checked in state.items()),
            input_widget,
            widgets.Label(value=f"Number of unfinished todo{plural}: {num_remaining}"),
        ]


IPWTodoApp()

This alternative implementation also misses out on some of Pret's features:

  • the app stops working if the server shuts down
  • hover events cannot be listened to
  • no React dom diffing: the app must either be re-rendered entirely (as in the example), or you must determine specifically which field of which widget to update

docs.title: Use it in a standalone app
docs.text:
You can also use pret to build standalone web applications. Copy the above code in a file named app.py, and change the last line to

if __name__ == "__main__":
    run(TodoApp)

Then, run the following command, and voilà !

python app.py

docs.title: How Python components run in the browser
docs.text: When you display a Pret component in a notebook, the function you wrote does not run in the kernel but in the browser, every time React renders it. Running it in Python would mean a round trip to the kernel for each click or keystroke. This page explains how Pret makes this work: how the Python code becomes JavaScript, how the values it uses travel with it, what a notebook output actually contains, and how the browser calls back into Python when a function has to run there.

docs.title: Components are React function components
docs.text:
Pret follows the model of React: a component is a function that returns elements, and React calls it again whenever its state changes. Elements such as div and button from pret.react, and hooks such as use_state, are Python stubs whose browser version calls React directly. For instance, use_state is React's own useState. We will follow this component through the rest of this page:

from pret import component, use_state
from pret.react import button, div

greeting = "Hello"


def label(count):
    return f"{greeting}, clicked {count} times"


@component
def Counter():
    count, set_count = use_state(0)
    return div(button(label(count), on_click=lambda event: set_count(count + 1)))


Counter()

When you click the button, the state changes and React calls Counter again in the browser, which calls label again, without contacting the kernel.

docs.title: Python code is translated into JavaScript
docs.text:
Pyodide could run Python itself in the browser, but it has to download and start a full Python runtime, and every call between React and Python code would go through WebAssembly. Pret instead translates the functions to JavaScript with Transcrypt, so that they run as fast as ordinary JavaScript and call React directly.

To do so, Pret needs the source of each function. It reads it with inspect.getsource when possible. Otherwise, for instance for a lambda, whose source line also contains the code around it, or for a function created with exec, it rebuilds the source from the bytecode with pygetsource. Transcrypt then turns label into the following code, keyword argument handling aside:

var label = function (count) {
return '{}, clicked {} times'.format(greeting, count);
};

A few standard modules come translated in advance, such as math, re, datetime, json, itertools and functools. Functions from other modules cannot run in the browser: see Interacting with the server for these.

What differs from Python

The translated code keeps JavaScript semantics in a few places. An empty list or dict is true in an if, since Transcrypt turns if items: into if (items): test len(items) instead. value is None becomes value === null, which does not match the undefined that JavaScript returns for a missing prop or key.

docs.title: Captured values travel with the function
docs.text:
A function rarely stands alone: label reads the global greeting, and Counter calls label, div, button and use_state. Pret finds the names a function reads from outside, its globals and closure variables, and wraps the function in a factory that receives them as arguments. The factory name holds the ID of the kernel's CBOR stream described below, 45c6b961 here, and the name of the function:

def pret_factory_45c6b961_label_0(greeting):
    def label(count):
        return f"{greeting}, clicked {count} times"

    return label

The factory is translated once, and the captured values are sent next to it. The browser then recreates the function by calling the factory with these values. Since Counter captures label, which is itself a function, label is sent the same way as one of the values of Counter's factory, and so on recursively, for functions, classes and objects alike.

These values are encoded with CBOR, a binary format close to JSON, extended with tags for the values JSON cannot describe. For instance, label becomes the tag 4000 holding its factory name and captured values, 72 bytes in all:

4000(["pret_factory_45c6b961_label_0", ["Hello"]])
Tag Python value Recreated in the browser by 4000 A function, as its factory name and captured values calling the factory with the values 4001 A class, as its name, bases, attributes and methods Transcrypt's class constructor 4002 An object with __reduce__, as a function and its arguments calling the function, for instance rebuild_dataframe for a DataFrame 4003 Another object, as its class and attributes creating an instance and setting its attributes

Why CBOR

Pickle can only be read by Python, and JSON has no way to tag a value or to send bytes. CBOR also keeps shared references: a Store used by two components is encoded once and remains a single object in the browser, where both components see the same edits. Finally, bytes travel as they are, which matters for a Store without sync, whose DataFrame rows are sent inside the CBOR data as Arrow bytes.

docs.title: What a notebook output contains
docs.text:
Displaying a component appends its values to a CBOR stream shared by the whole kernel, and its factories to a single JavaScript bundle. The notebook output only names that stream and the position of the component in it:

{"application/vnd.pret+json": {"detach": false, "view_data": {"marshaler_id": "45c6b961…", "chunk_idx": 3}}}

When the page displays this output, it asks the kernel for the bytes it has not received yet, along with the bundle, then decodes the component. Functions whose code was already sent, such as the functions of a cell run again, reuse their factory, so displaying a component again mostly sends new values.

This is also why an output saved in a notebook cannot be displayed after the kernel restarts: its stream no longer exists, and the cell has to be run again. An app started with pret.run serves the same data and bundle from its web server.

docs.title: Calling back into Python (@server_only)
docs.text:
Some functions have to run in Python, because they read files, query a database or use a library that has no browser version. Decorating them with server_only, as shown in Interacting with the server, keeps them in Python, and the browser receives a stub instead. When the function is called from the browser, the stub sends the call to the kernel as a message:

{"function_id": "…", "args": [42], "kwargs": {}, "callback_id": "…"}

The call returns a promise, which resolves with the result once the kernel has run the Python function. A server_only function therefore becomes asynchronous in the browser, even when it is a plain def in Python: browser code has to await its result. Since a component cannot wait while it renders, the call goes in an event handler or an effect, which stores the result in a state:

@server_only
def read_title(path):
    return Path(path).read_text()


@component
def Title():
    title, set_title = use_state("Loading…")

    async def load():
        set_title(await read_title("title.txt"))

    use_effect(load, [])
    return div(title)

Results go through JSON, except bytes, which are sent as binary buffers of the same message: a PDF returned by a server function, or a page of DataFrame rows as Arrow data, arrives in the browser as a Uint8Array without being converted to text.

The DataFrames of a connected Store use these calls for their queries, see How widgets query DataFrames. Store edits have their own messages, see What happens when you edit a Store.

docs.title: What happens when you edit a Store
docs.text: When a widget changes a connected Store, for instance when you tick a checkbox bound to store["todos"][0]["done"] or edit a cell of a DataFrame, the page shows the new value at once and sends the edit to the Python Store, which saves it. Every other page and notebook showing the same Store then receives the edit a moment later. This page follows such an edit from the page to Python and back, then explains what happens when the connection drops, when two people edit the same value, and how undo keeps the edits of others. Inside a Store file describes the SQLite tables mentioned below.

docs.title: Who takes part
docs.text:
Three parts are involved in an edit:

  • the Python Store, one per notebook kernel or Python process, which holds the current values, decides whether an edit is accepted, saves it and keeps the undo history of each page
  • the page controller, one per Store in each browser page, which shows edits at once, sends them to Python one at a time and applies the changes made elsewhere
  • the SQLite database, a file or an in-memory database, where Python saves each accepted edit as one revision

A Store created without sync never talks to Python: its edits stay in the page and cannot be undone. The rest of this page is about connected Stores, created with sync=True or a file.

docs.title: Two kinds of edits
docs.text:
A Store holds ordinary values, such as mappings, lists, strings and numbers, and DataFrames, and the page describes an edit of each differently. When you change an ordinary value, the page records operations on paths of the Store's JSON document: set for a mapping key or a list item, and insert and delete for list items. For example:

{"op": "set", "path": ["data", "todos", 0, "done"], "value": true}

A DataFrame cell cannot be named by a path, since the table is not part of the document and can be too large to be sent to the page anyway. The page names the row by its internal row ID instead, and lists the new values of its columns:

{"resource_id": "todos-id", "row_identity": 1, "values": {"done": true}}

Otherwise both kinds travel together: one widget action can change both, for instance a cell and the label of a filter, and Python saves them in the same revision. They only differ when someone else edited the Store in the meantime, as explained below.

docs.title: The page shows the edit at once
docs.text:
Waiting for Python before showing a click would make every widget feel slow. The page therefore applies the edit to its own copy of the values before Python answers, a technique known as optimistic update. Ordinary values are changed in the page's copy of the JSON document. DataFrame rows depend on how the page holds them for that Store:

  • with dataframe_sync="paged", the default, the page only has the rows it has already fetched, and shows the new values over them
  • with dataframe_sync="full", the page holds a SQLite copy of the tables and writes the edit to it inside a savepoint, so that local filters and sorts take it into account at once. Inserted rows get a temporary negative ID until Python assigns the real one

docs.title: The page sends one request
docs.text:
The page then sends both kinds of changes to Python as one request:

{
"request_id": "edit-42",
"origin": "page-a",
"kind": "edit",
"base_revision": 7,
"ops": [{"op": "set", "path": ["data", "todos", 0, "done"], "value": true}],
"edits": [{"resource_id": "todos-id", "base_revision": 7, "row_identity": 1, "values": {"done": true}}]
}
  • ops lists the operations on ordinary values, which may only change paths under "data"
  • edits lists the row edits
  • base_revision is the revision the page showed when the user made the edit
  • request_id lets the page send the request again if needed
  • origin identifies the page, whose undo history receives the edit

A page waits for the reply before sending another request, and a second local edit raises until then.

docs.title: Python checks and saves it
docs.text:
Other pages or notebooks may have saved revisions since base_revision, and the paths of the page operations can then point to the wrong item. Python therefore moves these operations over the newer revisions, as if the user had made them afterwards, a technique known as operational transformation:

Saved since base_revision Page operation What Python saves insert at ["data", "todos", 0] insert at ["data", "todos", 0] the page item after the saved one, both are kept insert at ["data", "todos", 0] set at ["data", "todos", 2, "done"] set at ["data", "todos", 3, "done"] set at ["data", "title"] set at ["data", "title"] the page value, the last writer wins delete at ["data", "todos", 2] set at ["data", "todos", 2, "done"] nothing, the request is a conflict

Python views such as todo = store["todos"][2] follow their item in the same way when items are inserted or deleted before it. DataFrame rows need no such transformation, since their IDs do not change when other rows are inserted or deleted: Python only checks that no later revision changed the same cell, or inserted or deleted the row, and rejects the edit otherwise.

When everything applies, Python saves the operations and the row changes as revision 8, in one SQLite transaction, and replies:

{"request_id": "edit-42", "status": "applied", "revision": 8, "row_identities": [[1]], "can_undo": true, "can_redo": false}

The page then replaces its optimistic values with the saved ones. In full mode, it rolls back to its savepoint and writes the accepted rows in the same step, then maps temporary row IDs to the saved ones, so that the table does not flash intermediate rows.

docs.title: Other pages catch up
docs.text:
Once the revision is saved, Python tells every page showing this Store that it changed:

{"sync_id": "store-id"}

Each page then asks for the revisions after the last one it applied. A page holding fetched rows also names their IDs, and receives their new values along with a summary of the other changes:

{"revision": 9, "commits": [{"revision": 9, "request_id": "edit-43", "origin": "page-b", "kind": "edit",
"ops": [{"op": "insert", "path": ["data", "todos", 0], "value": {"text": "tea"}}],
"changes": [{"resource_id": "todos-id", "kind": "update", "offset": 0, "length": 512}],
"summaries": [{"resource_id": "todos-id", "kind": "update", "columns": ["done"], "count": 1}]}]}
  • ops are applied as they are to the page's copy of the document
  • changes point to the Arrow data of the changed rows, sent with the message at the given byte offset
  • a summary tells a widget to query its rows again when a changed column is part of its filter or sort

In full mode the reply contains every changed row, which the page writes to its copy. If the page itself had a pending edit and Python accepted it unchanged, the page keeps the values it shows. Otherwise it cancels its optimistic values and applies the revisions in order.

Another Python process can also save revisions to the same file. Each process checks the file before each change and every 0.2 seconds while the Store is in use, applies the revisions saved by the others, then notifies its own pages in the same way. SQLite's lock makes two processes save their revisions one after the other.

docs.title: When the edit does not go through
The reply is lost
docs.text:
Python saves the edit before replying, so a lost reply does not mean a lost edit. The page keeps the edit pending and sends the same request_id again when the connection returns. Python finds the reply it saved for that request in _pret_acknowledgments and returns it, without applying the edit a second time.

In a notebook, all Pret outputs of a session share one connection to the kernel. It opens with the first Pret output and reconnects on its own as long as an output remains open, including in a hidden tab. When Python cannot be reached as the page loads, for instance on a static documentation page, the Store shows the values sent with the page and refuses edits until the connection returns.

docs.title: The edit is rejected
docs.text: When an operation or a row edit conflicts with a newer revision, or is invalid, Python saves nothing and replies with "status": "conflict" or "failed". The page then cancels its optimistic values, both the ordinary values and the table cells.

docs.title: Saving fails
docs.text: When SQLite itself fails while saving, nothing is saved either: Python restores the values the edit changed by applying the inverse of its operations, and keeps the page histories. If this restoration fails too, the Store refuses further edits.

docs.title: Undo and redo
docs.text:
Each page undoes its own edits only, without erasing what others changed since. To do so, Python records which revisions each page made, and every revision saves the inverse of its operations. Undo is sent like any other request:

{"request_id": "undo-7", "origin": "page-a", "kind": "undo", "base_revision": 9, "ops": [], "edits": []}

Python then restores the cells changed by the last edit of that page, except cells another page changed since, even to the same value. In the same transaction, it applies the inverse operations, transformed over the newer revisions, and skips the values another page changed since. Redo repeats only what undo restored, and the reply carries can_undo and can_redo for the page buttons.

Reloading a page gives it a new origin, so it starts with empty undo and redo lists. A notebook callback awaited by a page joins that page's history.

docs.title: DataFrame
docs.text:
Tabular data that can be placed in a PRET Store and displayed by widgets.

Create one from rows, an Arrow or pandas table, or a Spark or Ibis expression. The provider fetches rows from that source and applies edits when supported. Adding an Arrow or pandas DataFrame to a Store copies its rows into the SQLite database of that Store. Spark and Ibis expressions remain queries against their source until explicitly collected, for example by save_store.

docs.title: DataFrameProvider
docs.text:
Bases: ABC

Read a table for DataFrame widgets, with optional saving and editing support.

Subclasses implement describe and query. These methods can return their result directly or asynchronously, DataFrame awaits either form. A query returns an Arrow table containing the requested rows, not serialized bytes or SQL text.

Providers that support save_store also implement synchronous materialize. Editable providers implement apply_edit and report edit capability in describe.

docs.text:
Store a callback function that can be updated without re-rendering, and return a stable wrapped function that will always call the latest callback.

This can be used in two ways:

1) With dependencies (decorator factory):

@use_event_callback([dep1, dep2])
def the_callback(*args, **kwargs):
    ...

docs.title: use_imperative_handle
docs.text:
Safely binds a custom value or API to a parent's ref.

Unlike manually setting ref.current, this hook automatically handles the lifecycle: it updates the ref when dependencies change and cleans it up (resets it to None) when the component unmounts.

Use this to expose specific methods (like focus or reset) to a parent, rather than giving them direct access to internal DOM nodes.

from pret.react import button, div, input


@component

    # 1. The internal ref connects to the actual DOM element
    internal_input_ref = use_ref(None)

    # 2. We define what the parent is allowed to see/do and attach
    # that API to the handle passed down from the parent

        handle,
        lambda: {
            "reset_and_focus": lambda: (
                setattr(internal_input_ref.current, "value", ""),
                internal_input_ref.current.focus(),

        [],
    )

def App():
    # The parent creates a ref
    input_controller = use_ref(None)

    def on_click(event):
        # The parent calls the custom method defined in the child
        input_controller.current.reset_and_focus()

    return div(
        # Pass the ref as a regular prop named 'handle'
        CustomInput(handle=input_controller),
        button("Reset Form", onClick=on_click),

The view shows the scope of the DataFrame, the rows shared by all its widgets in the page, filtered and sorted for this component. When no scope is set, the hook loads the whole table. This hook exposes a rowSource for loaded data, the preceding rowSource while the view changes, and the DataFrame description, loading message, and error. It releases its view when the component unmounts. Pass arguments by position, the browser function takes no keywords.

To show related tables together, such as notes and their entities, pass load=False and set the scopes from a component effect. await dataframe.fetchScope(filter) queries the scope of a filter without showing it, dataframe.setScope(scope) shows it in every widget of that DataFrame. docs.title: use_event_callback

Store a callback function that can be updated without re-rendering, and return a stable wrapped function that will always call the latest callback.

This can be used in two ways:

1) With dependencies (decorator factory):

@use_event_callback([dep1, dep2])
def the_callback(*args, **kwargs):
    ...

2) or without

@use_event_callback  # (equivalent to @use_event_callback([]))
def the_callback(*args, **kwargs):
    ...

docs.title: StoreDoc
docs.text:
Keep the live values of a Store and save their edits as operations in its StoreDatabase.

edit_transaction groups Python edits, DataFrame edits and browser requests in one SQLite transaction, its operations and their inverses are saved together with the table changes. apply_browser_edit moves browser operations over the commits they did not see, refresh loads the commits saved by other processes. Each browser page has an undo history of its revisions, reversed selectively by reverse_action.

ATTRIBUTE DESCRIPTION root

Live tree, a MapNode with the user value under "data", the Store "metadata" and its sync "id"

database

StoreDatabase saving the operations, the current values and the DataFrame tables

TYPE: StoreDatabase | None

revision

Latest revision applied to root

histories

Undo and redo revisions per browser page origin

Operations and inverses of the open transaction, replayed backwards if it fails

docs.title: edit_transaction
docs.text:
Group Python, DataFrame and browser edits so SQLite saves them together as one revision.

If the block raises, the live values are restored by applying the recorded inverses, nothing is saved, and the uncommitted DataFrames are forgotten. Browser page origins, including their awaited Python callbacks, record the revision in the page undo history.

docs.title: rollback

Table cells are reversed selectively by StoreDatabase.reverse, and ordinary values by the inverse operations of the action moved over the later commits, skipping values another page changed since. The reversal is itself recorded in the opposite list, for redo or a new undo.

docs.title: StoreDatabase
docs.text:
Store the values and edit log of one Pret Store in SQLite.

Each _pret_changes row holds the operations of one revision on the ordinary values, their inverses and the SQL changes of its DataFrame tables. A transaction saves them together with one revision number and request ID. _pret_state holds the ordinary values as JSON at its revision, it is rewritten once the operations logged since exceed a tenth of its size and when the database closes, read_state replays the operations after it. The log records which cells changed and who changed them, so undo can preserve another user's edits and a repeated browser request can return its earlier result.

build_store attaches this database to StoreDoc, which sends updates to browsers after saving. SQLiteDataFrameProvider fetches and edits the table rows. DataFrame queries can also use an in memory database without a live document.

docs.text:

File to open, or :memory: for a Store that is not saved to disk

DEFAULT: ':memory:'

readonly

DEFAULT: False

Operations of the current transaction and their inverses, in the order they undo, set by StoreDoc

values

Live values after the current transaction, set by StoreDoc so _pret_state is rewritten without replaying

table_changes

TYPE: Session | None

docs.text:

keys maps each top-level Store key to its DataFrame resource ID. A key that clashes with another SQLite object, a reserved prefix or another key in a different case gets no view.

docs.title: read_state
docs.text: Return the current ordinary values and their revision, _pret_state with the operations logged after it

docs.title: write_state
docs.text: Rewrite _pret_state at the latest revision, from the live values when given or by replaying the log

docs.title: transaction
docs.text:
Save operations, table edits and one acknowledgement in one SQL transaction.

Nested calls join the outer transaction. If a block raises, none of its SQL changes are saved, StoreDoc restores the live values.

docs.title: browser_data
docs.text:
Send Arrow tables, or the operations and row changes of the commits after a revision.

Browsers call this once without a revision, receiving the current values and, for complete copies, every table, then with the last applied revision. Byte offsets identify Arrow streams in the response buffer. Newly created tables are copied at the final revision, so their earlier row changes are excluded from this response. With watched resource IDs and row IDs, only subscribed row values are sent, alongside summaries for query maintenance.

docs.title: acknowledgment

Row identities are a scalar for one row, a list for a DataFrame batch or grouped lists for a browser transaction that edits several DataFrames.

docs.text: Create a new store that can be used to store and synchronize data between various components of the app, between a server and its clients, or between different processes (or across multiple runs of the app) using a file.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
PARAMETER DESCRIPTION data

Initial data to store in the document. It can be a dictionary, list, or any simple value. If a callable is provided, it will be called to get the initial data. This can be useful if the initial data is expensive to create, and you only want to create it if the store is actually being initialized with it (e.g. when using file synchronization and the file doesn't already exist).

dataframe_sync

Paged queries by default, or full to copy every SQLite table to connected browsers

DEFAULT: 'paged'

dataframe_max_bytes

Required positive Arrow byte limit for the initial full copy download

DEFAULT: None

sync

There are three options for this parameter:

  • If false, this store will not be synchronized between a server and its clients. This can be useful for local-only stores, like style management.
  • If true, the store will be synchronized between a server and its clients. Any changes made to the store will be sent to the server and vice versa.
  • If a path is provided, the store will be synchronized with the file at this path. Any changes made to the store will be written to the file, and any changes made to the file will be read into the store. This can be useful if you want to persist the store to disk or share it between different processes (think servers or kernels).

TYPE: Optional[Union[bool, str, PathLike]] DEFAULT: None

docs.title: pret.store_ops
docs.text:
JSON operations on Store values, their inverses, and their transforms over concurrent operations.

Ordinary Store values are a JSON tree. Every edit is a list of operations on paths from the root, eg

{"op": "set", "path": ["data", "todos", 0, "done"], "value": true}
{"op": "insert", "path": ["data", "todos", 2], "value": {"text": "Buy milk", "done": false}}
{"op": "delete", "path": ["data", "filters", "label"]}

Map keys are str and list indices int, so the last path element tells whether an operation targets a map key or a list position. Python applies browser operations over the commits they did not see with transform_seq, and reverses a commit with its inverse operations transformed the same way, see pret/store.py.

docs.title: StoreOpError
docs.text:
Bases: ValueError

An operation does not apply to the current Store value, eg its path no longer exists

docs.title: Conflict
docs.text:
Bases: ValueError

A browser operation targets a value that a later commit removed or replaced

docs.title: validate
docs.text:
Return a plain JSON copy of a value assigned to a Store, refusing values a browser cannot represent.

Tuples become lists, numbers outside the exact JavaScript integer range and non finite floats are refused.

docs.title: clone

docs.title: resolve

docs.title: child_at

docs.title: apply
docs.text:
Apply one operation in place and return its inverse.

make builds the tree value from the operation value and its new container, the live Store uses it to create nodes, a copy is stored otherwise. The inverse holds the removed objects themselves, so applying it restores the same containers.

docs.title: is_list_position

docs.title: transform
docs.text:
Express a, defined on the same value as b, after b was applied.

Returns the moved operation, or None when a no longer applies, and flags among "drop" (b already did what a does), "invalid" (b removed or replaced the value a targets) and "touch" (both changed the same value). a_later decides which of two inserts at the same position goes first.

docs.title: shape_inverse
docs.text: Return an operation with the opposite effect on list positions, to move later operations past a skipped one

docs.title: transform_seq
docs.text:
Move a sequence of operations over committed operations that it did not see.

committed items are operations with the "origin" of their commit. In "rebase" mode, used for browser requests, an operation whose target was removed or replaced raises Conflict and the last writer wins otherwise. In "undo" mode, used to reverse a commit, operations whose target another origin changed later are skipped, so the reversal keeps the edits of other pages.

docs.title: DataFrames
docs.text:
• pret.DataFrame values can be stored in a Store. Records, pandas and Arrow tables are copied to SQLite and editable, Ibis and Spark queries stay in their source and are read only (apply_ibis_filter, custom DataFrameProviders).
  • Browsers receive pages of rows (dataframe_sync="paged", the default) or a complete copy (dataframe_sync="full" with dataframe_max_bytes). Edits are checked row by row, an edit based on a row another user changed since is refused as a conflict.
  • use_dataframe_view subscribes a component to a filtered and sorted view of a DataFrame.

docs.title: Saving Stores
docs.text:
• save_store and load_store write and reopen a Store, its DataFrames and its edit history as one SQLite file. Its tables and views are readable with plain SQLite, ordinary values are a JSON document in _pret_state.
  • load_store_snapshot returns plain Python values, DataFrames as in memory copies of their rows.
  • Store files of earlier releases are converted the first time they are opened, which needs pip install 'pret[legacy]', the original is kept as name.legacy.

docs.title: Store values and collaboration
docs.text:
• Store values no longer use Yjs or pycrdt. They are a JSON tree changed by small operations, set, delete and insert on paths. Python decides every edit: concurrent list insertions are all kept, an edit under a value removed by a newer commit is refused, the last write wins on the same key.
  • pret-pycrdt is now the optional legacy extra and yjs is no longer bundled.
  • Undo and redo are kept per browser page and skip values another page changed since, see use_store_history. Awaited Python callbacks of a page join its history.
  • A failed save restores the previous values and keeps the undo history.
  • A captured value, eg todo = store["todos"][2], keeps following its item when items are inserted or removed before it, in Python and in the browser.

docs.title: Breaking changes
docs.text:
• subscribe(store, callback) now calls callback(ops, change), where ops are the JSON operations under the watched value, eg {"op": "set", "path": [0, "done"], "value": True}. It returns a function that unsubscribes.
  • Store values must be JSON values. Integers must be within ±(2^53 - 1), NaN and infinities are refused, tuples become lists, and browser BigInt values become numbers.
  • In compiled browser code, key in store_mapping is now false for missing keys, list.push returns the new length and splice returns the removed items.
  • ipykernel 7.0 to 7.3 are excluded, they can leave browser requests unread so pages stop following their kernel (ipykernel#1529).

docs.title: Other changes
docs.text:
• python -m pret.testing run --suite python|client|jupyter|all runs Python, browser and JupyterLab tests, --coverage merges Python and TypeScript coverage. Extensions such as Metanno reuse it through [tool.pret.testing].
  • JupyterLab and standalone bundles are built in production mode, standalone apps share pret with extensions.
  • Fix sorted and list.sort in transpiled code, which are now stable and compare tuples item by item.
  • Fix an async use_effect leaving its Promise as React cleanup.
  • Server functions returning bytes send them as binary, received as a Uint8Array.
  • Bundles are serialized safely, views rendered again reuse their browser code, Joy views follow the JupyterLab theme.
  • cbor2 is pinned below 5.8, which fails to decode Pret bundles.
  • With ipykernel 7.4 and JupyterLab 4.6, Pret requests are no longer dropped once the subshell of the request that loaded a Store is deleted, eg after a Metanno view is reloaded.

docs.title: v0.6.3 (2026-05-08)
docs.text:
• Avoid Transcrypt's silent failures by calling it as a subprocess instead of importing it.
  • Synchronized stores should now be more effective at blocking writes while disconnected or while sync is blocked and roll back unsaved pending changes on disconnection.
  • Such disconnections now trigger a state synchronization upon connection recovery.
  • In Jupyter, we now better detect app disconnections by listening to global jupyter service connection failure signals.
  • In Jupyter, we should better recover/attach comms on disconnected or already running notebooks.
  • The use_connection_status hook is now notified (state_write_rejection_count and last_state_write_rejection fields) when the user tries to edit a synchronized state in a disconnected app.
  • @component can now be used as a decorator factory (@component()) and accepts memo=True to wrap the generated React element in React.memo.
  • Standalone bundles now store serialized data and generated code separately, and Jupyter bundle transfers now send binary bundle chunks with optional gzip compression : this should make the initial loading of components faster and more reliable in bad network scenarios.
  • Full page mode now hides the underlying jupyter UI elements, preventing user actions from editing the notebook

docs.title: v0.6.0 (2026-02-26)
docs.text:
• Added a new load_store_snapshot function to load a Python snapshot of the store state without subscribing to updates or risking mutations. This can be useful for instance in Metanno to load the annotations in a read-only pure Python format for export or processing purposes.
  • We now warn users when they call create_store with initial data and a file already exists at the specified path, to prevent accidental overwriting of existing data.
  • create_store now also accepts data as a callable that returns the initial data, to support lazy initialization of the store state.
  • Jupyter outputs now send only marshaler_id/chunk_idx and fetch bundles on demand. This should reduce the notebooks file size drastically for apps containing large amounts of data, and speed up the rendering of outputs.
  • New "Open in a new browser tab" command on Pret widgets in jupyter to create a new full-viewport view that overlays and hides jupyter simple presentation mode.
  • New "Restart app" button when widget is detected as stale or kernel is down upon widget mounting
  • Rendering a pret widget now autosaves the notebook to limit the kernel-notebook desynchronization issues
  • All tutorials are now runnable notebooks, rendered identically as documentation pages
  • New transact function to group mutations as a single transaction.

docs.title: v0.4.0 (2025-08-19)

  • Fixed prepack command that didn't collect used js modules

docs.title: v0.3.0 (2025-07-01)
docs.text:
• Add file system persistence for stores, using concatenations of yjs/pycrdt update binaries. Using file watchers, this also enables collaboration between multiple users using different servers/kernels.
  • Renamed proxy(..., remote_sync=...) to create_store(..., sync=...) to better reflect the purpose of the function.
  • Fixed front end to support large binary updates

docs.title: v0.2.0 (2025-06-10)
docs.text:
• Major change: I dropped pyodide and replaced it with Python → JavaScript transpilation (using Transcrypt) on the server. This comes with a few caveats such as the lack of support for some Python constructs and modules (to be documented), but brings a lot of benefits:

    • Runtime performance: the runtime is now much faster, as it runs in JavaScript the browser and does not require a converting Python objects to JavaScript objects and back.
    • First-time load: the first-time load is now much faster, as we don't require to load the Pyodide runtime and the Python standard library in the browser.
    • Portability: pret can now run without Internet access, as it does not require to load the Pyodide.
    • Error handling: errors (and any thrown object) are now bubbled outside Python and can be handled in JavaScript, which allows for better error handling, as well as throwing Promises to support React Suspense.

  • Pret tracked proxies are now marshaled as valtio and proxies in the browser: it is no longer possible to mutate the state using the output of use_store_snapshot.

  • Dropped old custom valtio-like python state management, and use (pret-)pycrdt instead
  • Added dependency to pret-pycrdt, fork of pycrdt to support identity preservation and therefore pickling, required for our marshaling mechanism
  • Improved notebook-kernel pret manager synchronization and resynchronization

docs.title: v0.1.0 (2025-03-20): Initial release
docs.text: Pret is a library for building full-stack reactive user interfaces in Python, using React as a rendering engine.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: pip install pret pret-joy

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
• Python, only Python: pret is written in Python: you can write your both your UI and server actions Python. No need to learn a new language, or to use a transpiler.
  • Client-side rendering: unlike other Python UI frameworks, pret runs primarily in the browser. This enables a fast response time to user actions (like hover events), and a better user experience under degraded network conditions.
  • Built on React: pret uses React as a rendering engine, and benefits from its ecosystem.
  • Reactive: unlike other solutions like ipywidgets, pret is reactive. Only the parts of the UI that need to be updated are re-rendered.
  • State management: in addition to React's local state management (i.e. use_state), pret provides a global and modular state management solution that is synchronized both between components, and between the client and the server.
  • Modular: pret is designed to be modular. You can easily create your own components, and reuse them in other pret-based projects.
  • Integrated with Jupyter: pret components can be used in Jupyter notebooks, as well as in standalone web applications.
  • Remote execution: pret can call and use the result of Python functions on the server from the browser

docs.title: Connection status
docs.text: use_connection_status() lets your components react to connectivity changes. You can use it to display the connection status and inform users about the app state.

docs.title: Connection info
docs.text:
The hook returns a reactive status object with fields such as:

  • connected: True, False, or None (unknown)
  • reason: a short machine-readable reason
  • transport: e.g. jupyter-comm, standalone-http, websocket
  • kernel_connection_status: Jupyter kernel connection status when relevant
  • last_error: last transport/send error if any
  • state_write_rejection_count: number of rejected writes to synchronized stores
  • last_state_write_rejection: details about the latest rejected synchronized-store write

Whenever these values change, components using the hook re-render automatically.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
from pret_joy import Box, Button, Stack, Typography

from pret import component, create_store, use_connection_status, use_store_snapshot
from pret.react import h4, p, span

# Local-only store: never needs a backend connection.
local_state = create_store({"count": 0})

# Synced store: requires a live server/kernel counterpart to persist/synchronize updates.
synced_state = create_store({"count": 0}, sync=True)


def increment_local(event):
    local_state["count"] = local_state["count"] + 1


def increment_synced(event):
    synced_state["count"] = synced_state["count"] + 1


@component
def ConnectionStatusDemo():
    status = use_connection_status()
    local = use_store_snapshot(local_state)
    synced = use_store_snapshot(synced_state)

    # fmt: off
    return Stack(
        [
            h4("Connection status"),
            Box(
                span("connected:"), span(str(status["connected"])),
                span("reason:"), span(status["reason"]),
                span("transport:"), span(status["transport"]),
                span("kernel_connection_status:"), span(status["kernel_connection_status"]),
                span("last_error:"), span(status["last_error"]),
                span("state_write_rejection_count:"), span(str(status["state_write_rejection_count"])),
                span("last_state_write_rejection:"), span(str(status["last_state_write_rejection"])),
                style={
                    "display": "grid",
                    "gridTemplateColumns": "1fr 1fr",
                }
            ),
            h4("Update behavior"),
            p(f"Local store count (always local): {local['count']}"),
            Button("Increment local store", on_click=increment_local),
            p(f"Synced store count (requires backend): {synced['count']}"),
            Button("Increment synced store", on_click=increment_synced),
            p("While disconnected, the synced store keeps its last values and refuses edits. Local updates still apply."),
        ],
        spacing=1.25,
        sx={"m": 1, "width": "100%"},
    )
    # fmt: off


ConnectionStatusDemo()

On this documentation page there is no Python kernel behind the demo. The status shows the failed request to the server, the synced store keeps the values sent with the page, and each click on its button is refused and counted in state_write_rejection_count, while the local store still works. Run the notebook to see the synced store follow your clicks.

Here is how a simple status message can be customized depending on the connection status.

from pret_joy import Stack, Typography

from pret import component, use_connection_status


@component
def ConnectionAwareMessage():
    status = use_connection_status()

    connected = status["connected"] is True
    text = "Remote sync is available." if connected else "Running without remote sync (offline/local-only mode)."

    return Stack(
        [
            Typography("Connection-aware message", level="title-lg"),
            Typography(
                text,
                level="body-md",
                color=("success" if connected else "warning"),
            ),
        ],
        spacing=1,
        sx={"m": 1, "width": "100%"},
    )


ConnectionAwareMessage()

docs.title: Your first component
docs.text:
Let's create a first UI component with Pret. We will start simple, with the "Hello World" of UI components: a Todo list.

Pret is a declarative UI library, which means that you describe the UI you want, and Pret takes care of rendering it for you. Under the hood, we use React and React libraries to render the UI.

docs.title: Composing components
docs.text:
Our app should be able to display a list of todos, where each todo is described by a text and a boolean indicating whether it is done or not. Let's use Joy's Checkbox for this:

from pret_joy import Checkbox

Checkbox(
    label="My first todo",
    checked=True,
    sx={"m": 1},
)

Great ! We successfully declared and rendered our first component. Let's make it a list. We will use the Stack component to stack multiple components vertically. To compose components, we pass checkboxes as positional arguments (or a list) to the Stack component, and Pret will render them as children of the Stack component.

from pret_joy import Checkbox, Stack

Stack(
    Checkbox(label="My first todo", checked=True),
    Checkbox(label="My second todo", checked=False),
    sx={"m": 1},
)

Instead of hardcoding the todos, we can use a list of todos and a loop to render them:

from pret_joy import Checkbox, Stack

todos = [
    {"text": "My first todo", "done": True},
    {"text": "My second todo", "done": False},
]

Stack(
    [Checkbox(label=todo["text"], checked=todo["done"]) for todo in todos],
    spacing=2,
    sx={"m": 1},
)

We can turn this into a TodoList component, so that we can reuse it later:

from pret_joy import Checkbox, Stack

from pret import component


@component
def TodoList(todos):
    return Stack(
        [Checkbox(label=todo["text"], checked=todo["done"]) for todo in todos],
        spacing=2,
        sx={"m": 1},
    )


TodoList(todos=todos)  # (1)!
  1. Here, todos are not children components but parameters of the TodoList component, also known as props in React, so we pass them as keyword arguments. In fact, passing them as positional arguments would raise an error.

You can also write @component() when you want to pass options to the decorator. For components with expensive renders and stable props, @component(memo=True) wraps the generated React component with React.memo.

docs.title: Reacting to events
docs.text:
Now that we have a list of todos, we want to be able to mark them as done or not. We can use the on_change event of the Checkbox component to react to changes. For now, let's just make a popup appear when a todo is checked or unchecked.

from pret_joy import Checkbox, Stack


def on_change(event):
    checked = event.target.checked
    alert(f"Todo {'checked' if checked else 'unchecked'}")


Checkbox(
    label="My first todo",
    checked=True,
    on_change=on_change,
    sx={"m": 1},
)

docs.title: Adding state
docs.text:
Our app is still a bit static : you may have noticed that you cannot change the value of the checboxes. We need to add state to our app to keep track of the todos' state. Let's start simple by making a Counter component that increments a counter each time a button is clicked. We can use the use_state hook, which allows us to create a state variable that will persist across renders (calls of our component) and trigger a re-render when its value changes.

from pret_joy import Button, Stack, Typography

from pret import component, use_state


@component
def Counter():
    count, set_count = use_state(0)

    def increment(event):
        set_count(count + 1)

    return Stack(
        [
            Button("Increment", on_click=increment),
            Typography(f"Count: {count}"),
        ],
        spacing=2,
        sx={"m": 1},
    )


Counter()

As you can see, every time you click the button, the state changes which triggers a re-render of the component. This is how we can make our TodoList component interactive. We will use the use_state hook to keep track of the todos' state.

from pret_joy import Checkbox, Stack

from pret import component

todos = [
    {"text": "My first todo", "done": True},
    {"text": "My second todo", "done": False},
]


@component
def TodoList(todos):
    todos, set_todos = use_state(todos)

    def on_change(event, index):
        new_todos = list(todos)
        new_todos[index] = {**todos[index], "done": event.target.checked}
        set_todos(new_todos)

    return Stack(
        [
            Checkbox(
                label=todo["text"],
                checked=todo["done"],
                on_change=(lambda index: lambda event: on_change(event, index))(index),
            )
            for index, todo in enumerate(todos)
        ],
        spacing=2,
        sx={"m": 1},
    )


TodoList(todos=todos)

docs.title: Work with DataFrames
docs.text:
A Store (cf Sharing state) can hold lists and dictionaries, but what if your data is a pandas DataFrame, or a Spark query over millions of rows ? Converting everything into a list of dicts and sending it to the browser would be expensive.

Put a pret.DataFrame in the Store instead. Widgets then request the rows they display, filtering and sorting run where the rows live, and edits are checked row by row. What you can do with it depends on where the rows come from

You add Rows live in Editable ? Records, pandas or Arrow A SQLite copy owned by the Store Yes A Spark or Ibis query The original source No, it is a read-only view of the query A query result saved with save_store The SQLite file of the saved Store Yes

docs.title: A small editable table
docs.text:
Run this notebook with Pret and Metanno installed, Metanno supplies the table widget.

import pandas as pd

from pret import DataFrame, create_store

todos = pd.DataFrame(
    [
        {"todo_id": 1, "text": "My first todo", "done": True},
        {"todo_id": 2, "text": "My second todo", "done": False},
        {"todo_id": 3, "text": "My third todo", "done": False},
    ]
)
store = create_store({"todos": DataFrame(todos)}, sync=True)

sync=True connects browser edits to this Python session.

# Documentation pages have no Python kernel, they show the table below with a browser only Store
store = create_store({"todos": DataFrame(todos)})

from metanno import DataWidgetFactory

factory = DataWidgetFactory(store)
factory.create_table_widget(
    store_key="todos",
    primary_key="todo_id",
    fields=[
        {"key": "todo_id", "kind": "text"},
        {"key": "text", "kind": "text", "filterable": True},
        {"key": "done", "kind": "boolean", "editable": True},
    ],
    style={"height": "200px"},
)

Check a box, then read the rows from Python

store["todos"].materialize().to_pandas()
todo_id text done 0 1 My first todo True 1 2 My second todo False 2 3 My third todo False

materialize() collects the rows as an Arrow table, to_pandas() converts it. Now finish the second todo from Python

store["todos"].update(identity={"todo_id": 2}, values={"done": True})
store["todos"].materialize().to_pandas()
todo_id text done 0 1 My first todo True 1 2 My second todo True 2 3 My third todo False

The checkbox of the second todo changes in the table. identity names the row by a column value, so sorting or filtering the table does not change which row is edited.

docs.title: Where did the edits go ?
docs.text:
print(todos["done"].tolist())
print(store["todos"].materialize()["done"].to_pylist())

[True, False, False]
[True, True, False]

The pandas table is unchanged. When you added it, Pret copied its rows into a SQLite database owned by the Store, and edits change that copy. SQLite is a database stored in a single file, here kept in memory, so the edits last as long as the Store. Save the Store to keep them in a file.

docs.title: Browse a query without copying it
docs.text:
A Spark DataFrame or an Ibis table describes a query, its result can be too large to collect. Pret keeps it connected to its source: widgets send their filters and sorts to the source and receive a preview of at most 500 rows. This Ibis example needs pip install 'ibis-framework[duckdb]'

import ibis

backend = ibis.duckdb.connect()
backend.create_table("todos", todos)
query = backend.table("todos")
external = create_store({"todos": DataFrame(query)}, sync=True)

DataWidgetFactory(external).create_table_widget(
    store_key="todos",
    primary_key="todo_id",
    fields=[
        {"key": "todo_id", "kind": "text"},
        {"key": "text", "kind": "text", "filterable": True},
    ],
    source_requery=True,
    style={"height": "200px"},
)

DataFrame(spark_df) works the same way. These query DataFrames are read-only, the source database is never modified.

docs.title: Make an editable copy of a query
docs.text:
Select what you want to work on, then save it

from pret import save_store

unfinished = query.filter(~query.done)
preview = create_store({"todos": DataFrame(unfinished)}, sync=True)
saved = save_store(preview, "unfinished-todos.pret", bounds={"todos": {"max_rows": 100}})
saved["todos"].update(identity={"todo_id": 3}, values={"done": True})
saved["todos"].materialize().to_pandas()
todo_id text done 0 2 My second todo False 1 3 My third todo True

save_store runs unfinished, copies its rows into unfinished-todos.pret and returns a Store connected to that file, where they are editable. max_rows rejects a larger result instead of truncating it, filter the query to choose the rows.

docs.title: How much data reaches the browser ?
docs.text:
A connected Store sends pages of rows as the table scrolls, after filtering and sorting them where they live. Lists and dictionaries are sent whole, they remain the simplest choice for small collections and application values.

Next, save and reopen the Store. To use DataFrames in your own components, or connect another kind of source, see How widgets query DataFrames.

docs.title: From notebook to app
docs.text:
In this tutorial, we build a small Todo app in a notebook and turn it into a standalone-ish app in two ways:

  1. Copy the code into a Python file and run it as a standalone app.
  2. Keep it in JupyterLab and open the Pret output in a dedicated browser tab.

docs.title: Build a dummy Todo app
docs.text:
from pret_joy import Checkbox, Input, Stack, Typography

from pret import component, create_store, use_state, use_store_snapshot

todos_store = create_store(
    {
        "Write docs": True,
        "Ship feature": False,
    },
)


@component
def TodoApp():
    todos = use_store_snapshot(todos_store)
    typed, set_typed = use_state("")
    num_remaining = sum(not done for done in todos.values())
    plural = "s" if num_remaining > 1 else ""

    def on_key_down(event):
        if event.key == "Enter" and typed.strip():
            todos_store[typed.strip()] = False
            set_typed("")

    return Stack(
        *(
            Checkbox(
                label=todo,
                checked=done,
                on_change=lambda event, t=todo: todos_store.update({t: event.target.checked}),
            )
            for todo, done in todos.items()
        ),
        Input(
            value=typed,
            on_change=lambda event: set_typed(event.target.value),
            on_key_down=on_key_down,
            placeholder="Add a todo",
        ),
        Typography(f"{num_remaining} unfinished todo{plural}"),
        spacing=2,
        sx={"m": 1, "maxWidth": 420},
    )


TodoApp()

docs.title: Interacting with the server
docs.text: In this tutorial, we'll see the difference between server-side and client-side code in Pret, and how to interact with the server from your app.

docs.title: Client-side environment
docs.text:
When you build a Pret app, you are building a web application that will run in the browser. By default, in Pret, any function used in a rendered component will be transpiled into javascript (including its scoped variables), then sent to the browser for execution. While this is a powerful feature, this means that this function doesn't have access to your server-side environment, such as your database, filesystem or computing resources. Moreover, the transpilation process has some limitations: you won't be able to import modules beside the ones provided by Pret, and you won't be able to use some Python features such as decorators, context managers, multithreading, etc.

For instance, let's take a look at the following component:

import time

from pret import component
from pret.react import br, div

static_time = str(time.time())


def dynamic_client_time():
    return str(time.time())


@component
def ShowCurrentWorkingDirectory():
    return div(
        f"Current time when this App was built: {static_time}",
        br(),
        f"Current CLIENT time when this App is rendered: {dynamic_client_time()}",
        style={"margin": "1em 0"},
    )


ShowCurrentWorkingDirectory()

The "dynamic" displayed time will be the one from the browser's. In fact, these docs are hosted as a static website on GitHub Pages, so there is no server-side environment to access during the rendering process. The "static" time will be the one from the server-side environment, computed when the component is built and sent as a constant to the browser.

docs.title: Running server-side code
docs.text:
To tell Pret to run a function on the server-side, you can decorate a function with @server_only. In this case, any call to this function from a client-side function will actually trigger a call to the server, and the result will be sent back to the client asynchronously.

Async functions

Any function decorated with @server_only becomes an async function from the client's perspective. This means that you must use await on the result of this function to get the actual return value.

At the moment, it is not possible to directly await the result of the server function in the rendering function. Therefore, in the example below, we combine @server_only with use_effect to update the displayed current server working directory once it has been fetched from the server.

import time

from pret import component, server_only, use_effect, use_state


@server_only
def dynamic_server_time():
    time.sleep(4)
    return str(time.time())


def dynamic_client_time():
    return str(time.time())


static_time = str(time.time())


@component
def ShowCurrentWorkingDirectory():
    server_time, set_server_time = use_state(None)

    async def on_load():
        set_server_time(await dynamic_server_time())

    use_effect(on_load, [])

    return div(
        f"Current time when this App was built: {static_time}",
        br(),
        f"Current CLIENT time when this App is rendered: {dynamic_client_time()}",
        br(),
        f"Current SERVER time when this App is rendered: {server_time or 'Waiting for server...'}",
        style={"margin": "1em 1em"},
    )


ShowCurrentWorkingDirectory()

docs.title: Synchronizing browser and Python values
docs.text:
The Sharing state example shares a Store between browser components. Without sync=True, a browser edit does not update the Store variable in your notebook.

Add sync=True to keep edits synchronized in both directions. Try clicking the counter, then reading and changing its value from another notebook cell.

from pret_joy import Button

from pret import component, create_store
from pret.hooks import use_store_snapshot

store = create_store(
    {
        "count": 0,
    },
    sync=True,
)


@component
def Counter():
    tracked = use_store_snapshot(store)

    def increment(event):
        store["count"] += 1

    return Button(
        f"Count: {tracked['count']}. Click to increment",
        on_click=increment,
        sx={"m": 1},
    )


Counter()

In your notebook, you can now change the store["count"] variable in another cell, and observe the change in the browser. Conversely, you can click the "Increment" button in the browser, and print the store["count"] variable in your notebook to see the change.

Offline app

We defined our store as synced with a server : since you are likely seing this in a github pages documentation, there is no server to sync to, or said otherwise, the server is currently unreachable. To avoid having users thinking their changes are saved, disconnected apps automatically rollback any changes made to a synchronized store. This is the reason why you cannot change the counter of the above app in the public documentation. To "unlock" it in offline mode, comment "sync=..."

# Show the current count, synchronized with the browser
print(store["count"])

# Change the count from the notebook
store["count"] = 42

docs.title: Save and reopen the Store
docs.text:
sync=True connects the browser and Python, but does not save a file. To keep the counter across kernel restarts, start it with a file path. The function supplies initial values only when the file is new.

store = create_store(lambda: {"count": 0}, sync="./shared_state.pret")

Pret writes changes to a SQLite database at that path. Other notebooks opening the same file receive its committed changes. For a complete example with editable tables, see Save and reopen your work.

docs.title: Read the current values without following later edits
docs.text:
For this counter Store, load_store_snapshot returns a plain Python dictionary. It does not subscribe to changes or write edits back to the file.

from pret import load_store_snapshot

snapshot = load_store_snapshot("./shared_state.pret")
print(snapshot, type(snapshot))

docs.title: Save and reopen your work
docs.text: A Store created with sync=True shares changes with Python, but disappears when its session ends. Let's save one and check that an edit survives reopening it.

docs.title: Save a Store
docs.text:
Run this in a notebook, using a new filename for the first save

from pret import DataFrame, create_store, load_store, save_store

store = create_store(
    {
        "title": "My todos",
        "todos": DataFrame(
            [
                {"todo_id": 1, "text": "My first todo", "done": True},
                {"todo_id": 2, "text": "My second todo", "done": False},
            ]
        ),
    },
    sync=True,
)
saved = save_store(store, "todos.pret")

todos.pret is a SQLite database, a file containing the Store's values, table rows and saved edit history. No separate database server is needed.

save_store returns a new Store connected to that file. Use saved in subsequent code and widgets. The original store remains separate. Saving to an existing filename raises FileExistsError, so rerun the next section with load_store when the file already exists.

docs.title: Edit and reopen it
docs.text:
saved["title"] = "Weekend todos"
saved["todos"].update(identity={"todo_id": 2}, values={"done": True})

reopened = load_store("todos.pret")
print(reopened["title"])
print(reopened["todos"].materialize().to_pylist())

Weekend todos
[{'todo_id': 1, 'text': 'My first todo', 'done': True}, {'todo_id': 2, 'text': 'My second todo', 'done': True}]

The title is Weekend todos, and the second todo has done=True. Changes made through saved or reopened are written to the file automatically. There is no second save call after each edit. You can run the load_store lines in a fresh Python session and see the same result.

For a pandas result, use reopened["todos"].materialize().to_pandas(). This collects the current rows, so select a manageable dataset before exporting a large table.

docs.title: Start directly with a saved Store
docs.text:
You can also create or reopen a Store in one call

todo_list = create_store(lambda: {"title": "My todos", "remaining": 0}, sync="my-todos.pret")

The function supplies the initial data only when the file is new. If my-todos.pret already exists, Pret loads its saved contents. This also works with DataFrames built from records, pandas or Arrow. For Spark and Ibis queries, use the explicit editable copy workflow. Attaching a live query to a saved Store does not save its source rows or database connection.

docs.title: What is inside the file?
docs.text:
todos.pret is a SQLite database, any SQLite tool can open it

import sqlite3

with sqlite3.connect("todos.pret") as connection:
    print(connection.execute("SELECT * FROM todos").fetchall())
    print(connection.execute("SELECT json_extract(value, '$.data.title') FROM _pret_state").fetchone())

[(1, 'My first todo', 1), (2, 'My second todo', 1)]
('Weekend todos',)

The todos DataFrame is readable as a SQL view of the same name, where done is stored as 0 or 1. Ordinary values such as title are not columns, they are part of one JSON document, which SQLite reads with json_extract.

Read the file with SQL, but edit it through Pret, so that connected notebooks and widgets see the change and undo keeps working. Inside a Store file explains where each kind of value is stored and what the other _pret_ tables are for.

docs.title: Save related changes together
docs.text:
Suppose finishing a todo also changes the list title. Group both edits with transact

from pret.store import transact

with transact(saved):
    saved["todos"].update(identity={"todo_id": 1}, values={"done": False})
    saved["title"] = "Todos to redo"

This group is a transaction. Pret commits both changes to SQLite together, then notifies other connected views. If the block fails, Pret restores the previous values.

docs.title: Open the same work in another notebook
docs.text:
Run load_store("todos.pret") in another notebook on the same filesystem. Each notebook has its own Python Store, and Pret watches the shared file for committed changes. An edit in either notebook updates the other Store and its connected widgets.

Both notebooks must use the same file. Copying todos.pret elsewhere creates a separate dataset, which does not continue synchronizing with the original.

docs.title: Read a copy without connecting
docs.text:
load_store_snapshot(path) returns a Python copy of the values without subscribing to updates. DataFrames in the copy hold their rows in memory, use materialize() to read them.

from pret import load_store_snapshot

copy = load_store_snapshot("todos.pret")
print(copy["title"], copy["todos"].materialize().num_rows)

Todos to redo 2

To edit these tables in a JupyterLab tab, continue with Metanno's walkthrough.

docs.title: Sharing state
docs.text: Our todo list can display and change its own values. Now let's add a second component that counts the unfinished todos. Checking a box should update both views.

docs.title: The state management problem
docs.text:
Why is state management hard in web development? The dynamic nature of user interfaces means multiple components must reflect and react to shared and changing data without re-rendering everything anytime something changes (e.g, you recompute the whole app UI whenever a single state variable changes), or convoluted data flows (e.g., state being passed through many layers of components that don’t even use it). Traditional approaches, like Redux, often introduce layers of boilerplate and require careful architecture when planning mutations on the app data.

There is another issue of immutability: we cannot mutate the state directly (e.g., state.todos[0]["done"] = True), since React, and thus Pret, often relies on shallow comparison to detect changes in the state. For instance, if todos is the same object, even though its content has changed, some React utils (e.g. memo) will consider that the state has not changed and will not trigger a re-render.

And if we take care of preventing direct mutations, changing the state can be cumbersome. For instance, if we want to change the done field of the first todo, we would have to do something like this:

new_todos = list(todos)
new_todos[0] = {**todos[0], "done": True}

# We now have todos != new_todos and
# todos[i] == new_todos[i] for all i except 0

docs.title: Pret's Store
docs.text: We need one place to keep the data they share. Pret calls it a Store. You can read and modify its lists and dictionaries with familiar Python operations, and components that use those values update automatically.

docs.title: Create a Store
docs.text:
Start with a few todos and a list of letters. The callback below prints the operations each change saves, with paths relative to the watched value. A Store can also synchronize with the browser, the Python session and a file, we will add those connections after sharing data between components.

from pret.store import create_store, subscribe

store = create_store(
    {
        "todos": [
            {"text": "My first todo", "done": True},
            {"text": "My second todo", "done": False},
        ],
        "letters": ["a", "b"],
    }
)


def on_event(ops, change):
    for op in ops:
        print(op["op"], op["path"], op.get("value"))


subscribe(store, callback=on_event)

store["todos"][1]["done"] = True

set ['todos', 1, 'done'] True

del store["todos"][1]["done"]

delete ['todos', 1, 'done'] None

store["todos"][1]["cool"] = True

set ['todos', 1, 'cool'] True

store["letters"].append("c")

insert ['letters', 2] c

store["letters"][1] = "z"

['letters'] => [{'retain': 1}, {'delete': 1}, {'insert': ['z']}]

Ordinary Store values include dictionaries, lists, strings, numbers, booleans and None. For tables, use Pret DataFrames, introduced in a later tutorial.

docs.title: Using stores in components
docs.text:
The use_store_snapshot hook reads the Store values used by a component. When those values change, Pret renders that component again. Let's use it to display the todo list.

from pret_joy import Checkbox, Stack

from pret import component, create_store, use_store_snapshot

store = create_store(
    {
        "todos": [
            {"text": "My first todo", "done": True},
            {"text": "My second todo", "done": False},
        ],
    }
)


@component
def TodoList():  # (1)!
    todos = use_store_snapshot(store["todos"])

    def on_change(event, i):
        store["todos"][i]["done"] = event.target.checked

    return Stack(
        [
            Checkbox(
                label=todo["text"],
                checked=todo["done"],
                on_change=lambda event, i=i: on_change(event, i),
            )
            for i, todo in enumerate(todos)
        ],
        spacing=2,
        sx={"m": "1em"},
    )


TodoList()
  1. Both widgets will read the same Store through use_store_snapshot.

docs.title: Sharing state between components
docs.text:
Display this counter in a second cell, keeping the todo list visible above it. Then check a box in the list, the counter changes too.

from pret_joy import Typography

from pret.react import br


@component
def RemainingTodoCounter():
    todos = use_store_snapshot(store["todos"])
    num_remaining = sum(not todo["done"] for todo in todos)

    return Typography(
        f"Number of unfinished todos: {num_remaining}.",
        br(),
        "Click todos in the previous component to change the count.",
        sx={"m": "1em"},
    )


RemainingTodoCounter()

The Store tracks changes to lists and dictionaries, so you can modify them directly. The snapshot gives React a new value when the data read by the component changes. You do not have to copy every enclosing list or dictionary yourself.

These widgets share data in the browser. To also read their edits from Python, continue with Synchronizing browser and Python values. Pret exchanges ordinary state changes as small JSON operations, eg {"op": "set", "path": ["todos", 0, "done"], "value": true}. Saved Stores keep them in SQLite alongside any DataFrame rows.

docs.title: Group several changes
docs.text:
The button below checks all todos at once. Without grouping, each assignment sends its own change notification. With transact(store), Pret groups the assignments and notifies subscribers once after the block.

Try both modes and compare the log below the buttons.

from pret_joy import Button, Checkbox, Radio, RadioGroup, Stack, Typography

from pret import (
    component,
    create_store,
    use_effect,
    use_event_callback,
    use_state,
    use_store_snapshot,
)
from pret.store import subscribe, transact

store = create_store(
    [
        {"text": "My first todo", "done": False},
        {"text": "My second todo", "done": False},
        {"text": "My third todo", "done": False},
    ]
)


@component
def TodoList():
    todos = use_store_snapshot(store)
    logs, set_logs = use_state([])
    mode, set_mode = use_state("no-tx")

    is_all_checked = all(t["done"] for t in todos)
    button_all_txt = "Check all" if not is_all_checked else "Uncheck all"

    @use_event_callback
    def on_todo_change(event, i):
        store[i]["done"] = event.target.checked

    @use_event_callback
    def on_click(event):
        if mode == "tx":
            with transact(store):  # <------ this line right here !
                for todo in store:
                    todo["done"] = True if not is_all_checked else False
        else:
            for todo in store:
                todo["done"] = True if not is_all_checked else False

    @use_event_callback
    def on_store_change(ops, change):
        set_logs(lambda logs: [*logs, " | ".join(op["op"] + " " + str(op["path"]) for op in ops)])

    @use_effect(dependencies=[])
    def on_mount():
        return subscribe(store, on_store_change)

    checkboxes = [
        Checkbox(
            label=todo["text"],
            checked=todo["done"],
            on_change=lambda e, i=i: on_todo_change(e, i),
        )
        for i, todo in enumerate(todos)
    ]

    return Stack(
        [
            RadioGroup(
                Radio(value="no-tx", label="Without transact"),
                Radio(value="tx", label="With transact"),
                orientation="horizontal",
                name="mode",
                value=mode,
                on_change=lambda event: set_mode(event.target.value),
                sx={"justifyContent": "center"},
            ),
            Stack(
                Button(button_all_txt, on_click=on_click, sx={"flex": "1"}),
                Button("Reset logs", variant="outlined", on_click=lambda: set_logs([])),
                direction="row",
                spacing=1,
            ),
            *checkboxes,
            Stack([Typography(log, level="body-sm") for log in logs], spacing=1),
        ],
        spacing=2,
        sx={"m": "1em"},
    )


TodoList()
