docs.title: TicTacToe
docs.text:
Let's build a simple TicTacToe game using Pret. We will build a simple game where two players can play against each other.

from pret import component, create_store
from pret.hooks import use_store_snapshot
from pret.react import button, div
from pret.store import transact

state = create_store(
    {
        "board": [0] * 9,
        "turn": 1,
        "winning_pattern": [],
    },
)

winning_patterns = [
    [0, 1, 2],
    [3, 4, 5],
    [6, 7, 8],
    [0, 3, 6],
    [1, 4, 7],
    [2, 5, 8],
    [0, 4, 8],
    [6, 4, 2],
]

SQUARE_STYLE = {
    "display": "flex",
    "justifyContent": "center",
    "alignItems": "center",
    "width": "60px",
    "height": "60px",
    "margin": "2px",
    "fontSize": "24px",
    "padding": "0",
    "appearance": "none",
    "border": "1px solid grey",
}

WINNING_SQUARE_STYLE = {
    **SQUARE_STYLE,
    "background": "lightGreen",
}

GRID_STYLE = {
    "display": "grid",
    "gridTemplateColumns": "repeat(3, 66px)",
    "gridGap": "2px",
    "margin": "1em 0",
}


@component
def TicTacToe():
    tracked = use_store_snapshot(state)
    winning_pattern = tracked["winning_pattern"]

    def on_click_square(idx):
        # if the game is over, clean everything on click
        with transact(state):
            if bool(state["winning_pattern"]) or 0 not in state["board"]:
                state["board"][:] = [0 for _ in range(9)]
                state["winning_pattern"] = []
                return

            # place a piece on the board
            value = state["board"][idx]
            if value == 0:
                state["board"][idx] = state["turn"]
            state["turn"] = 2 if state["turn"] == 1 else 1

            # check for victory
            for pattern in winning_patterns:
                players = set(state["board"][i] for i in pattern)
                if len(players) == 1 and 0 not in players:
                    state["winning_pattern"] = pattern

    return div(
        [
            button(
                "X" if square == 2 else "O" if square == 1 else "",
                on_click=lambda event, idx=idx: on_click_square(idx),
                style=(WINNING_SQUARE_STYLE if idx in winning_pattern else SQUARE_STYLE),
            )
            for idx, square in enumerate(tracked["board"])
        ],
        style=GRID_STYLE,
    )


TicTacToe()

docs.title: Widgets
docs.text: Self-contained, interactive and controllable components.

docs.title: What’s a widget?
docs.text:
In Pret, a widget is a component that manages its own UI state, exposes a small imperative API (a “handle”) for commands like scroll to X or focus, and emits events (callbacks) when the user interacts with it. A widget runs on its own, without needing to be controlled by a parent component.

In dashboards and multi-pane tools, panes often look at the same data from different angles but don’t need to mirror each other’s UI details (scroll positions, hovers, transient filters, typing...): this is where widgets shine, as they encapsulate their own UI state and logic.

By contrast, a classic (controlled / presentational) component, such as AnnotatedText, keeps minimal or no state and expects its parent to hold all the UI logic and state and to pass it down as params.

docs.title: If it looks like a widget and quacks like a widget...
docs.text: Widgets are not a formal class or type in Pret. They are just components that can run without being controlled by a parent. Just like any other component in Pret, widgets can be declared from inside a @component function (i.e., controlled by another component) or directly from your notebook/server. To interact with other parts of the UI, widgets expose two kinds of interfaces:

docs.title: 1) Events (callbacks)
docs.text:
• Notify when an event occurs: on_change(id), on_hover(id, ...), ...
  • These are callbacks: they don’t change other widgets directly.

docs.title: 2) Imperative handle (commands)
docs.text:
• Let other parts of the UI command this widget: handle.current.scroll_to_id(id), handle.current.set_active(id), handle.current.set_filter(key, value), ...
  • These are UI actions and read-only getters like handle.current.get_selection().

Actions object

In Pret, a common pattern is to pass a mutable handle Ref defined with use_ref that the widget fills: it writes callable entries under a current attribute, which the parent can then call imperatively.

docs.title: Do's and don'ts
docs.text:
• Don’t wrap them in a stateful parent that is going to re-render often.
  • Don't make them expect props that change with the app state (e.g., value).
  • You can compose them in a layout/panel/div for presentational purposes.
  • You can control them from the notebook or from other widgets through their handle.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Our objective is to define a counter and a log that stand alone, and from the notebook decide if and how they talk to each other, without introducing a new "controller" (or "App") component. Controlled components (ie, non widgets components) push you to create a shared parent to pass props around. Widgets keep their own state, expose a small actions handle, and emit events so you can wire them together (or not) from the notebook.

Let's create a CounterWidget that exposes reset / set commands and an on_change event, and a LogWidget that exposes an add command.

from pret_joy import Button, Stack, Typography

from pret import component
from pret.hooks import use_event_callback, use_imperative_handle, use_ref, use_state


@component
def CounterWidget(handle=None, on_change=None):
    count, set_count = use_state(0)

    use_imperative_handle(
        handle,
        lambda: {
            "reset": lambda: set_count(0),
            "set": set_count,
        },
        [],
    )

    @use_event_callback
    def increment():
        def update(prev):
            new_value = prev + 1
            if on_change is not None:
                on_change(new_value)
            return new_value

        set_count(update)

    return Button(
        f"Count: {count}",
        on_click=increment,
        spacing=1,
        sx={"minWidth": 220, "m": 1},
    )


@component
def LogWidget(handle=None):
    messages, set_messages = use_state([])

    use_imperative_handle(
        handle,
        lambda: {
            "add": lambda text: set_messages(lambda prev: [*prev, text]),
            "clear": lambda: set_messages([]),
        },
        [],
    )

    return Stack(
        [
            Typography("Logs:", level="body-md"),
            *[Typography(f"- {msg}", level="body-sm") for msg in messages],
        ],
        spacing=1,
        sx={"minWidth": 220, "m": 1},
    )

Let's render the counter widget in a cell:

# remote refs to hold the counter actions
counter_handle = use_ref()
log_handle = use_ref()

CounterWidget(
    handle=counter_handle,
    on_change=lambda v: log_handle.current.add(f"Counter is now {v}"),
)

Then the log widget in another cell:

LogWidget(handle=log_handle)

Finally the reset button in another cell:

Button(
    "Reset counter",
    on_click=lambda: counter_handle.current.reset(),
    color="neutral",
    variant="outlined",
    sx={"minWidth": 220, "m": 1},
)

We could also have everything in the same cell using a Stack or Grid layout.

You can observe that no UI state is shared between the two widgets: they talk and synchronize through events and commands.

docs.title: Remote refs
docs.text:
In the example above, we created two use_ref() references in the notebook to hold the handles of the two widgets. When these refs are created in the notebook, they are called remote refs because they are created on the server side and allow to control widgets running on the client side. use_ref is the only hook that can be used outside of a @component function, i.e., directly in the notebook.

One advantage of this is that, should you refactor your app and move the widget creation from the notebook to a component, and the remote ref to a standard local ref, you just have to move everything in a @component function, and it should work like a charm.

However, this comes with a few limitations :

  • you can only interact with fields on the handle that are functions (e.g., handle.current.focus()), not properties (e.g., handle.current.value).
  • calling functions on remote refs is asynchronous, and the result is a future/promise. You cannot expect to get a return value immediately.

docs.title: Widget factories
docs.text:
For tables, Pret already supplies a DataFrame interface and Metanno supplies connected widgets, see Work with DataFrames. The examples below explain the factory pattern by manually copying a small pandas table and writing its callbacks. Use Pret DataFrames for paged queries, shared edits and saved tables.

As explained above, widgets are just components that follow some conventions. They should therefore not require access to the server/kernel state to be rendered. You may still need to configure a widget with some data from the server. This is where widget factories come in handy: a widget factory is a function that takes runs on the server and returns a Renderable widget that can be embedded in a Pret app.

For instance, imagine a DataFrame widget that displays the content of a pandas DataFrame. DataFrame are not serializable, so the widget cannot directly use a dataframe during its rendering. Instead, we can create a widget factory that takes a DataFrame, prepares the data (e.g., serializes it to JSON) and returns a Table configured with this data.

Observe how the factory function DataFrameComponentFactory is not decorated with @component: it is instead meant to run on the server and return a widget, which in turn can be rendered on the client.

Here is a component factory that takes a pandas DataFrame and returns a Table Renderable element:

import pandas as pd
from metanno import Table

from pret.render import Renderable


def DataFrameStaticViewFactory(df: pd.DataFrame, editable_columns=[]) -> Renderable:
    # Prepare the data (e.g., serialize to JSON)
    data = df.to_dict(orient="records")
    columns = [
        {
            "name": col,
            "key": col,
            "filterable": True,
            "kind": "text" if df.dtypes[col].kind in "iufc" else "boolean" if df.dtypes[col].kind == "b" else "text",
            "editable": col in editable_columns,
        }
        for col in df.columns
    ]

    # Return a Table component configured with the data
    return Table(rows=data, columns=columns)

Note that since Table expects the data to be prepared and updated for it by its caller (i.e., it is a controlled component), we have no way make this component dynamic.

Now, here is a widget factory that takes a DataFrame and returns a configurable metanno Table widget. It will expose an imperative API to set/get filters and scroll to a given row and an event callback when a cell is changed:

import pandas as pd

from pret import server_only
from pret.hooks import use_ref
from pret.render import Renderable, component


def DataFrameWidgetFactory(df: pd.DataFrame, handle=None, editable_columns=[]) -> Renderable:
    # Prepare the data (e.g., serialize to JSON)
    data = df.to_dict(orient="records")
    columns = [
        {
            "name": col,
            "key": col,
            "filterable": True,
            "kind": "text" if df.dtypes[col].kind in "iufc" else "boolean" if df.dtypes[col].kind == "b" else "text",
            "editable": col in editable_columns,
        }
        for col in df.columns
    ]

    @server_only
    def handle_cell_change_server(row_id, row_idx, col_key, new_value):
        df.at[row_idx, col_key] = new_value

    @component
    def Widget(handle=None, on_cell_change=None) -> Renderable:
        # Internal state
        filters, set_filters = use_state({})
        table_handle = use_ref()
        state_data, set_state_data = use_state(data)

        use_imperative_handle(
            handle,
            lambda: {
                "set_filters": set_filters,
                "get_filters": lambda: filters,
                "scroll_to_row_idx": lambda idx, behavior=None: table_handle.current.scroll_to_row_idx(idx, behavior),
            },
            [],
        )

        @use_event_callback
        def handle_filters_change(filters, col):
            set_filters(filters)

        @use_event_callback
        def handle_cell_change(row_id, row_idx, col_key, new_value):
            # Update local state to reflect the change
            updated_data = list(state_data)
            updated_data[row_idx] = {**updated_data[row_idx], col_key: new_value}
            set_state_data(updated_data)
            if on_cell_change is not None:
                on_cell_change(row_id, row_idx, col_key, new_value)

        # Return a Table component configured with the data and event handlers
        return Table(
            rows=state_data,
            columns=columns,
            filters=filters,
            auto_filter=True,
            on_filters_change=set_filters,
            on_cell_change=handle_cell_change,
            handle=table_handle,
            style={"height": "200px"},
        )

    return Widget(handle=handle, on_cell_change=handle_cell_change_server)

You can now use it by first creating a reference to hold the widget handle, then creating the widget using the factory, and finally rendering it:

df = pd.DataFrame([{"todo_id": i, "text": f"Todo {i}", "done": False} for i in range(100)])
handle = use_ref()
DataFrameWidgetFactory(df, handle=handle)

Again : like widgets, a widget factory merely a code pattern: it is a function that runs on the server and returns a Renderable widget that can be rendered and controlled from the outside. Note how changing a cell in the table updates the underlying DataFrame on the server side. You can also control it imperatively by running the following code in another cell:

# Scroll to row 50
handle.current.scroll_to_row_idx(50);

or from a button:

from pret_joy import Button

Button(
    "Go to row 50",
    on_click=lambda: handle.current.scroll_to_row_idx(50),
    sx={"m": 1},
)

docs.title: How widgets query DataFrames
docs.text:
A table widget can show a DataFrame of millions of rows, scroll through it, filter and sort it, although the browser never receives the whole table. This page explains how, starting from the questions you meet when a table grows or when your data lives somewhere Pret does not know

  • What does a widget ask Python for, and where does the filtering run?
  • Can a small table be sent to the browser once, instead of page by page?
  • Why does a Spark or Ibis table show only 500 rows, and how to page through all of them?
  • How to connect another kind of source, such as an API or a database Pret does not support?

Start with Work with DataFrames if you have not added a DataFrame to a Store yet.

docs.title: A widget asks for pages
docs.text:
Every DataFrame has a provider, the Python object that runs queries on its rows. A widget never reads the rows directly. It sends a query describing the rows it needs, and the provider returns them as an Arrow table. You can send the same query yourself

from pret import DataFrame, create_store

store = create_store(
    {
        "todos": DataFrame(
            [
                {"todo_id": 1, "text": "Buy bread", "done": True},
                {"todo_id": 2, "text": "Call the plumber", "done": False},
                {"todo_id": 3, "text": "Water the plants", "done": False},
                {"todo_id": 4, "text": "Book a table", "done": False},
            ]
        )
    }
)
result = store["todos"].provider.query(
    {
        "filter": {"kind": "predicate", "column": "done", "operator": "eq", "value": False},
        "sort": [{"column": "text", "direction": "asc"}],
        "offset": 0,
        "limit": 2,
    }
)
print("Matching rows", result["total_count"])
result["table"].to_pandas()

Matching rows 3
__pret_row_id todo_id text done 0 4 4 Book a table False 1 2 2 Call the plumber False

The query asks for the first two unfinished todos, sorted by text. The reply holds those two rows, and total_count, the number of rows matching the filter, which the widget uses to size its scrollbar. Each row also has __pret_row_id, the ID a widget sends back when the row is edited.

Query field Example Meaning filter {"kind": "and", "children": [...]} A tree of and, or, not and predicates. Predicates compare a column with eq, ne, lt, lte, gt, gte, in, contains, starts_with, ends_with, is_null or is_not_null sort [{"column": "text", "direction": "desc"}] Sort columns, in order of priority offset, limit 0, 256 The page to return, after filtering and sorting columns ["todo_id", "text"] Columns to return, all of them by default include_count false Skip computing total_count

The filter and the sort run where the rows live, before the page is cut

DataFrame built from Filtered and sorted by Records, pandas or Arrow, copied into the Store SQLite, in the Store file or in memory A Spark or Ibis query The source database or Spark cluster, through Ibis Your own provider Your code, see Connect another source

While the table scrolls, the browser requests pages of 256 rows aligned on multiples of 256, so that two overlapping scroll positions share the same request. It keeps at most 2048 rows in its cache. It already knows the count after the first query, so later pages pass include_count: false, which lets Spark and Ibis skip counting the rows again. When a source rejects a page as too large, the browser halves the page size until it fits, or reports the error if a single row is too large.

docs.title: Send a small table to the browser once
docs.text:
Each page is a round trip to Python. For a small saved Store, load_store can instead send the Store tables to the browser once

from pret import load_store

store = load_store("todos.pret", dataframe_sync="full", dataframe_max_bytes=10_000_000)

The browser loads the tables into its own SQLite database, so filtering, sorting and scrolling no longer wait for Python. Edits still go to Python, which checks and saves them, and the browser copy receives the saved rows. dataframe_max_bytes is required, and loading fails rather than sending more than that many bytes of Arrow data. This is not an offline mode, a page still needs its notebook kernel or server to save edits.

The three ways rows reach the browser

Store Rows reach the browser Filtering runs in Edits are saved by Connected, sync=True or a file, default dataframe_sync="paged" Page by page Python, or the Spark or Ibis source Python Connected, dataframe_sync="full" Once, when the page loads The browser Python Not connected, create_store(data) Inside the rendered page The browser Nobody, edits stay in the page

A Store without synchronization suits small examples and static pages, such as this documentation. Use a connected Store for large tables or for Spark and Ibis queries.

docs.title: Spark and Ibis queries show a preview
docs.text:
DataFrame(query) does not page through a Spark or Ibis source. It runs the query once, with a limit of 500 rows and no ordering, and widgets work on these loaded rows, the preview. Filters and sorts typed in a widget apply to the preview in the browser. To run the query again on the source with these filters, Metanno tables offer a query button, see source_requery=True in DataFrames. The widget shows the number of rows in the preview, not a total.

Counting and ordering a large Spark query can take as long as running it, a preview answers "what does this data look like" without paying that cost. When you need every row, page through the source instead

DataFrame(query), a preview DataFrame(provider=IbisDataFrameProvider(query, paging=True)), pages Rows a widget can reach The first 500 rows the source returns, in no particular order Every row, page by page Row count shown The size of the preview The total, counted by the source Widget filters and sorts Applied to the preview in the browser Run by the source, before paging Source queries One, when the preview loads or the query button is pressed A count, then one sorted query per page

In both cases, __pret_row_id is the position of a row in the current result, not a lasting ID. This is why these DataFrames are read-only. To edit or annotate rows, make an editable copy first.

This paged example needs pip install 'ibis-framework[duckdb]'

import ibis

from pret.dataframe_external import IbisDataFrameProvider

query = ibis.memtable({"todo_id": [1, 2, 3], "text": ["Buy bread", None, "Book a table"]})
paged = DataFrame(provider=IbisDataFrameProvider(query, paging=True))
result = paged.provider.query({"sort": [{"column": "text", "direction": "asc"}], "offset": 0, "limit": 2})
print("Matching rows", result["total_count"])
result["table"].to_pandas()

Matching rows 3
todo_id text __pret_row_id 0 2 NaN 0 1 3 Book a table 1

Pages are sorted by the requested columns, then by every other scalar column, so that the same row does not appear on two pages. Ascending sorts put nulls first, descending sorts put them last. To keep a preview but change its size, pass IbisDataFrameProvider(query, row_limit=2000) instead.

A raw Spark DataFrame needs pip install 'ibis-framework[pyspark]'. Pret registers it as a temporary Spark view, dropped when the DataFrame is released, and leaves the Spark session open with its settings. Rows are transferred as Arrow data, which keeps nullable integers and timestamp timezones.

docs.title: Show a DataFrame in your own component
docs.text:
Metanno's table widget is a Pret component, and your components can read DataFrames the same way with use_dataframe_view(dataframe, filter, primary_key, sort, load), with arguments passed by position. The hook returns

  • rowSource, with rowCount and getRows(start, end, signal), which fetches the rows of a range as described above
  • previousRowSource, the previous row source while a new filter or sort is loading, to keep showing rows
  • description, the column names and types, and loading and error messages to display

The row source works the same for the three Store modes above. The hook releases its query when the component unmounts.

All widgets showing one DataFrame in a page start from the same rows, its scope. For a Store table, the scope is a filter and the number of rows matching it. For a Spark or Ibis preview, it also holds the loaded rows. Each widget then adds its own filter and sort. When no scope is set, the hook loads the whole table.

Related tables need another start. A table of entities that follows a table of notes must show the entities of the listed notes, and change with them when the notes query changes. Pass load as False, and set the scopes from an effect of your component with two methods of the DataFrame

async def load_notes_and_entities():
    notes_scope = await notes.fetchScope(None)
    entities_scope = await entities.fetchScope(
        {
            "kind": "relation",
            "column": "note_id",
            "resource_id": notes.resource_id,
            "parent_column": "note_id",
            "filter": notes_scope.filter,
        }
    )
    notes.setScope(notes_scope)
    entities.setScope(entities_scope)

fetchScope(filter) queries a scope without showing it. The relation filter keeps the entities whose note_id appears in the notes matching the notes filter. setScope(scope) shows a scope in every widget of that DataFrame. Fetching both scopes before setting them keeps the two tables consistent, the entities table never shows the entities of notes that are no longer listed. Metanno's DataWidgetFactory loads its related tables this way.

docs.title: Connect another source
docs.text:
Pret already queries the databases supported by Ibis, through DataFrame(ibis_table). For another kind of source, such as a search engine or an HTTP API, write a provider. Subclass pret.DataFrameProvider and implement two methods

  • describe returns the columns, their Arrow types and the operations the source supports, for widgets to configure their fields
  • query receives the query fields above and returns the requested page as an Arrow table, with the total_count of matching rows, or None when include_count is false

Both methods may be synchronous or asynchronous. The provider should run the filter, the sort and the paging on its source, so that only the requested page reaches Python. Widgets also send a few more query fields. They read the row IDs of a range with "columns": ["__pret_row_id"], fetch selected rows with an in filter on these IDs, and send locate to scroll to a selected row. Query fields and return types are described in DataFrameProvider, and Pret's Ibis provider, dataframe_external.py, is a complete example.

Two optional methods add more. materialize collects every row, it lets save_store turn the source into an editable copy. apply_edit applies row edits, with "edit": True in the capabilities returned by describe. Without them, saving the Store and editing the rows raise an error.

docs.title: Inside a Store file
docs.text: Save and reopen your work creates todos.pret, edits it and reopens it. This page opens that file to answer a few questions. What does Pret write in it, and where? Can another tool read it? Why does a crash or a second notebook not corrupt it? And what are the _pret_ tables next to your data?

docs.title: What a Store holds
docs.text:
A Store holds three kinds of values, and the file saves each of them differently

Kind of value Example Saved as Ordinary values, mappings, lists, strings, numbers and booleans store["title"] = "My todos" One JSON document Editable DataFrames, built from records, pandas or Arrow DataFrame(pandas_df) One SQL table per DataFrame Source-backed DataFrames, built from a Spark or Ibis query DataFrame(spark_df) A reference only, the rows stay in the source

Each edit of any of them is also appended to an edit history, in the same file.

A .pret file is a SQLite database.

Why SQLite

SQLite keeps a whole database in one file and runs inside the Python process that opens it, so there is no database server to install or start. It also matches what a Store needs

  • Widgets filter and sort a table with SQL and receive only the rows they display, a large table is never loaded in memory
  • A widget edit can change an ordinary value and several rows, SQLite saves them in one transaction, either entirely or not at all, even if the process stops in the middle
  • Several notebooks or processes can open the same file, SQLite locks it while one of them writes
  • Any SQLite tool can read it, such as Python's sqlite3 module, pandas or DBeaver

A JSON or pickle file would be rewritten entirely at each edit and could not be shared between processes, and a Parquet file cannot be updated in place.

Let's open the file of the saving tutorial, or create it, with one ordinary value and one DataFrame

from pret import DataFrame, create_store

store = create_store(
    lambda: {
        "title": "My todos",
        "todos": DataFrame(
            [
                {"todo_id": 1, "text": "My first todo", "done": True},
                {"todo_id": 2, "text": "My second todo", "done": False},
            ]
        ),
    },
    sync="todos.pret",
)

and list what it contains

import sqlite3

connection = sqlite3.connect("todos.pret")
query = "SELECT type, name FROM sqlite_master WHERE type IN ('table', 'view') AND name NOT LIKE 'sqlite%'"
for kind, name in connection.execute(query + " ORDER BY type, name"):
    print(kind, name)

table _pret_acknowledgments
table _pret_changes
table _pret_dataframes
table _pret_revision_rows
table _pret_state
table data_todos_2e35342dffba
view todos

data_todos_… holds the rows of the todos DataFrame, and the todos view gives them a readable name. The _pret_ tables hold everything else. The next sections go through them in the order of the table above.

docs.title: Ordinary values, one JSON document
docs.text:
_pret_state has a single row. Its value column holds the whole Store as one JSON document, except the rows of its DataFrames. Each DataFrame is replaced by a reference to its SQL table, {"__pret_dataframe_ref__": "<resource ID>"}, and the document also holds the Store metadata and ID

print(connection.execute("SELECT value FROM _pret_state").fetchone()[0])

{"data":{"title":"My todos","todos":{"__pret_dataframe_ref__":"815a4b92bb244bcca30d19b6a84c50d7"}},"metadata":{},"id":"22bc0d63-e6cf-42c7-8b86-6ae82af0c039"}
  • data is the Store value, here the title and a reference to the todos DataFrame, whose rows are in the SQL table described in the next section
  • metadata holds the values passed to save_store(..., metadata=...), read them back with load_store_snapshot(path, metadata=True)
  • id identifies the Store, browser pages and other notebooks use it to follow its changes

Reading _pret_state and the DataFrame tables therefore gives the whole Store, as of the revision noted in _pret_state, see the note below. SQLite reads a single value with json_extract

connection.execute("SELECT json_extract(value, '$.data.title') FROM _pret_state").fetchone()

('My todos',)

This document can be a few edits behind

Rewriting the whole document at each edit would make editing a large Store slow. Instead, each edit appends its changes to the edit history, and _pret_state is rewritten only once these changes exceed a tenth of its size, and when the Store closes. Its revision column tells the last edit it includes.

Pret reads _pret_state and then applies the later edits, so load_store and load_store_snapshot always return current values. A plain SQLite reader can see values a few edits old while a notebook is editing the Store. DataFrame rows are always current.

docs.title: Editable DataFrames, one SQL table each
docs.text:
Adding records, a pandas table or an Arrow table to a Store copies its rows into a new SQL table, and _pret_dataframes lists these tables

connection.execute("SELECT resource_id, table_name, created_revision FROM _pret_dataframes").fetchall()

[('815a4b92bb244bcca30d19b6a84c50d7', 'data_todos_2e35342dffba', 1)]
  • resource_id is the ID used by references in _pret_state
  • table_name is the SQL table, named after the Store key with a random suffix, so that renaming the key or adding another DataFrame under the same key does not clash with it
  • arrow_schema, not shown, is the Arrow schema of the DataFrame, used to restore column types
  • created_revision is the edit that created the table

The SQL table has one more column than the DataFrame, __pret_row_id, an integer that identifies each row even when the DataFrame has no unique column. Pret uses it to edit a row, undo an edit or follow a row across notebooks. To read the rows, use the view named after the Store key, which has the DataFrame columns only

import pandas as pd

pd.read_sql("SELECT * FROM todos", connection)
todo_id text done 0 1 My first todo 1 1 2 My second todo 0

Each top-level DataFrame of the Store gets a view. If two keys refer to the same DataFrame, there are two views over one table, and an edit through either key changes the same rows

store["weekend"] = store["todos"]
connection.execute("SELECT name, sql FROM sqlite_master WHERE type = 'view'").fetchall()

[('todos', 'CREATE VIEW "todos" AS SELECT "todo_id","text","done" FROM "data_todos_2e35342dffba"'), ('weekend', 'CREATE VIEW "weekend" AS SELECT "todo_id","text","done" FROM "data_todos_2e35342dffba"')]

Deleting weekend would only drop its view. Renaming a key renames its view, the table keeps its name. DataFrames nested deeper in the Store get no view. Neither do keys that only differ in case from another key, since SQLite names ignore case, keys starting with sqlite_ or _pret_, and keys already used by another table.

Read with SQL, edit with Pret

A direct SQL write to these tables skips the edit history. Connected notebooks and widgets do not see it, and undo can then restore wrong values. The views cannot be written to.

Column types

SQLite has fewer types than pandas or Arrow. Pret stores each value as shown below, and restores the original type from the Arrow schema saved in _pret_dataframes

Arrow values Stored in SQLite as Booleans, signed integers and unsigned integers up to 32 bits INTEGER Floating point numbers REAL Strings and binary TEXT and BLOB Decimals and unsigned 64-bit integers Exact decimal TEXT Dates and times ISO TEXT with the declared precision Timestamps UTC ISO TEXT ending with Z Durations Signed integer count as TEXT, the unit is kept in the Arrow schema Structs, lists and maps JSON TEXT, maps as lists of key and value pairs

The Arrow schema keeps decimal scales, time units and original timezones. Inside JSON values, 64-bit integers, decimals and temporal values are strings, and binary values are base64. Pret compares exact numbers without converting them to floats, but a direct SQL ORDER BY on a TEXT column sorts as text, where "10" comes before "9".

docs.title: Source-backed DataFrames, a reference only
docs.text:
A Spark DataFrame or an Ibis table describes a query, and its result can be too large to copy. Pret keeps it as a query, so the file only holds a reference. This example needs pip install 'ibis-framework[duckdb]'

import ibis

source = ibis.memtable({"todo_id": [3], "text": ["My third todo"]})
store["remote"] = DataFrame(source)
print(connection.execute("SELECT json_extract(value, '$.data.remote') FROM _pret_state").fetchone())
print(connection.execute("SELECT count(*) FROM _pret_dataframes").fetchone())

('{"__pret_dataframe_ref__":"db68ecd432b74fa0a91a1a123f60a8bb"}',)
(1,)

_pret_state has a reference, but _pret_dataframes has no table behind it. The database connection and the query live in Python only, so reopening the file gives back the bare reference instead of a DataFrame

from pret import load_store

reopened = load_store("todos.pret")
reopened["remote"]

{'__pret_dataframe_ref__': 'db68ecd432b74fa0a91a1a123f60a8bb'}

The application must assign the query again, reopened["remote"] = DataFrame(source). To keep the rows themselves, make an editable copy with save_store, which runs the query and saves its result as an editable table, see DataFrames.

The same goes for application code. Metanno saves the name and parameters of the recipe that built an interface in the Store metadata, but the recipe's Python code and environment must be available when reopening.

docs.title: Edit history
docs.text:
Each saved change gets a revision number, 1 for the creation of the Store, then one per change. A change is one assignment, one DataFrame edit, one widget edit or one transact block. Pret saves everything a change does in one SQLite transaction, so the file never contains half of it. If the change fails, SQLite discards its writes and Pret restores the previous values in Python.

Let's change the title and a row in one transaction, then read the last revision

from pret.store import transact

with transact(store):
    store["title"] = "Todos for Sunday"
    store["todos"].update(identity={"todo_id": 1}, values={"done": False})

connection.execute(
    "SELECT revision, kind, origin, ops, inverse FROM _pret_changes ORDER BY revision DESC LIMIT 1"
).fetchone()

(4, 'edit', 'kernel-0bb8ee63dc224a38aafd1fb81a923917', '[{"op":"set","path":["data","title"],"value":"Todos for Sunday"}]', '[{"op":"set","path":["data","title"],"value":"My todos"}]')

Each row of _pret_changes describes one revision

  • ops lists the changes to the ordinary values, as set, insert and delete operations on paths of the JSON document, and inverse lists the operations that cancel them
  • changeset holds the old and new values of the changed rows, in SQLite's changeset format
  • origin names who made the change, this Python Store (kernel-…) or a browser page, kind tells whether the revision created the Store, applied an edit or undid one

Two smaller tables complete the history. _pret_revision_rows lists the row and columns each revision changed. When a browser sends an edit based on an older revision, Pret rejects it only if a later revision changed the same cell, or inserted or deleted the row. Undo also uses it to cancel the edit of one browser page while keeping the cells another page changed since.

_pret_acknowledgments keeps the reply sent for each request. If a browser loses its connection before receiving the reply, it sends the same request again, and Pret returns the saved reply instead of applying the edit twice.

This history is how several notebooks share one file. Each one checks the file every 0.2 seconds, and before each change, for revisions it has not applied yet, and applies their ops to its ordinary values. DataFrame rows need no copy, every notebook reads the same SQL tables. What happens when you edit a Store follows an edit from the browser to the file and to other pages.

History size and the journal file

The history is never pruned. Deleting _pret_changes rows is not a supported way to shrink a file.

todos.pret-journal is SQLite's rollback journal. SQLite manages it and can keep it after a commit, its presence does not mean that changes are unsaved.

docs.title: Files from older Pret versions
docs.text: Store files record their format number in PRAGMA user_version, 1 for this version. Files in the earlier binary format are converted to SQLite the first time create_store or load_store opens them, and the original is kept next to it as name.legacy. Converting them needs pip install 'pret[legacy]'. Close other notebooks using the file before opening it with this version, they would keep writing to the original. load_store_snapshot reads these files without converting them.
